So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss. In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss.     I arrived at a vastly inflated figure which was approved by the organisation, despite me raising concerns about the price not being in-line with our not-for-profit ethos. In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss. We were asked to put on a particular event for members which was to be ticketed.  The organisation I worked for asked me to set a ticket price before I had had the opportunity to fully price up the event.  I was pressurised into coming up with a figure.  In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss.     I arrived at a vastly inflated figure which was approved by the organisation, despite me raising concerns about the price not being in-line with our not-for-profit ethos. It felt wrong from the minute i sent the invite out.  <span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I lay awake at night, tossing and turning, unable to find peace as the weight of the decision to go along with the organisation bore heavily on my conscience. I knew this business had been a member for many years and was struggling with the downturn in economy and with new competition in town from larger retailers. In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss.     I arrived at a vastly inflated figure which was approved by the organisation, despite me raising concerns about the price not being in-line with our not-for-profit ethos. However, I was instructed to send out invites to the membership.  It felt wrong from the minute i sent the invite out.  <span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I lay awake at night, tossing and turning, unable to find peace as the weight of the decision to go along with the organisation bore heavily on my conscience. I knew this business had been a member for many years and was struggling with the downturn in economy and with new competition in town from larger retailers. I knew this business had been a member for many years and was struggling with the downturn in economy and with new competition in town from larger retailers.   However, I stuck to the line that I couldn't alter the price.  I was worried if I had done anything different I may lose my job. The organisation I worked for asked me to set a ticket price before I had had the opportunity to fully price up the event.  I was pressurised into coming up with a figure.  In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit. In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss.     I arrived at a vastly inflated figure which was approved by the organisation, despite me raising concerns about the price not being in-line with our not-for-profit ethos. However, I was instructed to send out invites to the membership.  It felt wrong from the minute i sent the invite out.  <span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I lay awake at night, tossing and turning, unable to find peace as the weight of the decision to go along with the organisation bore heavily on my conscience. The thought of potentially harming small businesses, who trusted us to support them, haunted me.  </span></p><p><span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I did realise that the businesses didn't have to buy tickets but I knew that many of them, particularly the smaller organisations felt they had to attend to be able to keep up with the networking opportunities such events provided.  </span></p><p><br></p><p>While tickets were being sold, I was given time to price up the event properly and found that we were selling tickets at nearly 35% over what we needed to break even.  I mentioned this to the organisation and they told me not to worry about it.</p><p><br></p><p>I then had a call from one of the very small independent traders who wanted to attend the event but wondered if there was any kind of discount available for smaller businesses.  I said I'd look into it confident that we could at least knock off the 35%.  However, I was instructed not to do that and to charge the full price.  I went back to the small business and told them that sadly I couldn't do anything about the price.  I felt really guilty doing this.  I knew this business had been a member for many years and was struggling with the downturn in economy and with new competition in town from larger retailers.   However, I stuck to the line that I couldn't alter the price.  I was worried if I had done anything different I may lose my job.    I had a few calls from the smaller businesses asking for discounts and questioning why prices were so high but stuck to the line that we were just covering costs.    </p><p>The event went ahead, many of the small businesses did attend and my bosses felt it had been a great success.  I was devastated to find that the excess profit went into unnecessary purchases of office furnishings and coffee making equipment for the management team.   A couple of weeks later I found out that 2 of the small businesses that had attended the event had decided to shut up shop.  They were significantly in debt and couldn't see any way out.  I felt and still feel that we contributed to that decisiiion.  I had several conversations with one of them who said they realised they could no longer compete when they struggled to attend networking events with big businesses and that going forward they would miss the support we offered.  I reported this back to the organisation, however they decided it was too bad and that they weren't prepared to change how they were pricing up events. The organisation I worked for asked me to set a ticket price before I had had the opportunity to fully price up the event.  I was pressurised into coming up with a figure.  In the past we had always priced tickets so that costs were just covered - the idea wasn't ever to make a profit.  So, in this instance I was already feeling bad about the fact we were guessing the ticket price.  I had to over estimate everything as I wasn't allowed to make a loss.     I arrived at a vastly inflated figure which was approved by the organisation, despite me raising concerns about the price not being in-line with our not-for-profit ethos. However, I was instructed to send out invites to the membership.  It felt wrong from the minute i sent the invite out.  <span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I lay awake at night, tossing and turning, unable to find peace as the weight of the decision to go along with the organisation bore heavily on my conscience. The thought of potentially harming small businesses, who trusted us to support them, haunted me.  </span></p><p><span style=\"background-color: rgb(238, 238, 238); color: rgb(51, 51, 51);\">I did realise that the businesses didn't have to buy tickets but I knew that many of them, particularly the smaller organisations felt they had to attend to be able to keep up with the networking opportunities such events provided.  </span></p><p><br></p><p>While tickets were being sold, I was given time to price up the event properly and found that we were selling tickets at nearly 35% over what we needed to break even.  I mentioned this to the organisation and they told me not to worry about it.</p><p><br></p><p>I then had a call from one of the very small independent traders who wanted to attend the event but wondered if there was any kind of discount available for smaller businesses.  I said I'd look into it confident that we could at least knock off the 35%.  However, I was instructed not to do that and to charge the full price.  I went back to the small business and told them that sadly I couldn't do anything about the price.  I felt really guilty doing this.  I knew this business had been a member for many years and was struggling with the downturn in economy and with new competition in town from larger retailers.   However, I stuck to the line that I couldn't alter the price.  I was worried if I had done anything different I may lose my job.    I had a few calls from the smaller businesses asking for discounts and questioning why prices were so high but stuck to the line that we were just covering costs.    </p><p>The event went ahead, many of the small businesses did attend and my bosses felt it had been a great success.  I was devastated to find that the excess profit went into unnecessary purchases of office furnishings and coffee making equipment for the management team.   A couple of weeks later I found out that 2 of the small businesses that had attended the event had decided to shut up shop.  They were significantly in debt and couldn't see any way out.  I felt and still feel that we contributed to that decisiiion.  I had several conversations with one of them who said they realised they could no longer compete when they struggled to attend networking events with big businesses and that going forward they would miss the support we offered.  I reported this back to the organisation, however they decided it was too bad and that they weren't prepared to change how they were pricing up events.
